🔍 DIAGNOSTICS TRAINER

Each circuit has been wired correctly but contains a single fault. Your job is to use the DVOM to diagnose the fault and identify its location.

Meter Modes: DC Voltage measures voltage in a live circuit. Resistance measures resistance with the circuit off. Continuity beeps when a path is complete. Use the mode buttons or click the dial.

Test Points: Click any yellow dot on the circuit to place a probe. Select RED or BLACK probe first, then click the test point.

Diagnosing: Click any component or wire segment on the circuit to select it as the fault location. Then click Submit Diagnosis.

Attempts: There is no limit on tries — keep testing until you find it. Getting it right on your 1st attempt earns 10 points, losing 1 point for each additional attempt, down to 0 points once you reach your 11th attempt. A hint is revealed after your 1st and 2nd incorrect attempts.

⚡ TYPES OF ELECTRICAL FAULTS

A quick reference for the fault types you'll run into in these circuits — what's happening electrically, how the customer experiences it, what you'd see during a visual inspection, and how the fuse or circuit breaker reacts.

Start with the load. Only three things can go wrong in a circuit: an open, unwanted (excessive) resistance, or a short (to ground or to power). Find the component that isn't working — the bulb, motor, relay coil, etc. Either that component has failed, or one of the wires connected to it has the wrong voltage. Figure out what each of its wires should read, then measure them. Even when there seem to be many problems, it is almost always one small defect causing all of the symptoms.
Fault Type What Happens Symptoms (How It Acts) Visual Signs (What to Look For) Protective Device Reaction
Short to Ground A live positive wire touches the metal vehicle frame or a ground wire before the load. Current takes a "shortcut" to ground with no load to limit it.
  • Component immediately stops working.
  • Replacement fuse blows immediately when power is applied.
  • A short that is blowing the fuse is always between the fuse and the load.
  • If a new fuse doesn't blow right away, the short may be intermittent — a fuse never blows for no reason.
  • Blown fuse (cloudy glass, broken element).
  • Melted wire insulation or smoke.
  • Scorch marks on the metal frame where the wire rubbed through.
  • Damaged insulation exposing bare wire copper.
 Fuse blows instantly, or an automotive circuit breaker trips and resets repeatedly (or stays open if it's a manual-reset breaker).
Short to Power A live positive wire touches another positive wire (usually from a different circuit), feeding voltage into the circuit from somewhere other than its own switch.
  • A component stays turned on constantly — the load will not turn off because the short is bypassing its switch.
  • Turning on one switch may activate a different accessory. (Before blaming a short, check for an open shared ground — see the look-alike note below.)
  • Copper wires melted or fused together inside a wiring harness.
  • Damaged insulation exposing bare wire copper.
  • Melted wire insulation or smoke.
 Usually no reaction (unless total current exceeds the fuse rating), but it causes "ghost" operation of the affected circuit.
Open Circuit A complete break in the circuit's path, stopping all current flow.
  • Component is completely dead; operating the switch has no effect.
  • Fuse remains intact.
  • The most common electrical fault — suspect it whenever a circuit won't turn on and the fuse is not blown.
  • With no current flowing, voltage doesn't drop, so everything between the break and the power source can read full voltage — even the ground side of the load ("phantom" voltage).
  • Severed or broken wire.
  • Disconnected harness plug.
  • Backed-out pins inside a connector terminal.
  • Loose, wobbly, or loose-fitting electrical connectors.
 No reaction. Fuses and breakers don't trip because current drops to zero.
Excessive Resistance Corrosion, loose connections, or undersized wire creates an unwanted restriction. That resistance "uses up" voltage that should have reached the load.
  • Component operates weakly (e.g., dim lights, slow power windows, slow-cranking starter).
  • Circuit works intermittently when wiggled or shaken.
  • Turn signals flash too fast or too slow, or a lamp-out warning appears on circuits the body control module monitors.
  • Moisture and corrosion in a bulb socket create heat that can distort the socket.
  • Green or white corrosion on battery terminals or ground points.
  • Loose, wobbly, or loose-fitting electrical connectors.
  • Discolored, heat-damaged plastic connector housings.
 Rarely trips. The extra resistance actually reduces current below the fuse rating, turning the restriction into an accidental heater instead.
Look-alike: short to power… or an open ground? If turning on one circuit makes a different circuit come on (or both work dimly), the likely cause is not two wires shorted together. It's usually an open ground shared by two circuits. Current from the switched-on circuit finds a path to ground back through the other circuit's load, creating a series circuit. This is called feedback, and it's common in lighting circuits that share ground connections. Check the ground connection of the circuit that didn't turn on.
A failed load looks like an open, too. A burned-out bulb, open motor winding, or open relay coil stops current just like a broken wire. If both wires at the load have the correct voltage (full power on one side, a good ground on the other) and it still doesn't work, the load itself is faulty. See "Checking the Load Itself" in the Diagnostic Testing Guide.

🔧 DIAGNOSTIC TESTING GUIDE

How to confirm each fault type with the DVOM — the meter setting to use, the procedure, and what a confirmed fault looks like compared with a normal, healthy reading.

Ground Rules for Every Test

  • Test on the car. Do your testing with everything installed and connected. Only remove a part once you've proven it faulty.
  • Start at the load, then divide and conquer. Measure the wires at the component that isn't working first. Next, decide whether the problem is on the power side or the ground side before checking switches, wires, and connections.
  • Voltage testing needs current flowing. Keep the circuit plugged in and switched on, and make sure your leads or back-probes make good contact. Voltage only drops across a resistance when current is flowing through it.
  • Change one variable at a time. Unplug, wiggle, or switch one thing, retest, and only then move on — otherwise you won't know which change made the difference.
  • Pick the strategy for the fault type. Opens and unwanted resistance are found with the voltmeter. Shorts that blow fuses are found by isolating sections of the circuit.
  • Verify before you replace. Confirm your diagnosis a second way, usually with a fused jumper wire (card 5), before replacing anything.

1. Short to Ground

The Goal: Find where power is escaping straight to the vehicle frame before it reaches the component. A short that is blowing the fuse is always between the fuse and the load.
Mode
Circuit breaker isolation first, then Resistance / Ohms (Ω) or Continuity (🔊) to confirm
Red Lead
VΩmA jack
Black Lead
COM jack
Narrow it down with a circuit breaker
  1. Install a new fuse of the same rating. If it doesn't blow, try to make it blow by operating the circuit and wiggling the harness.
  2. If it blows, replace it with a self-resetting circuit breaker of the same or lower rating. The breaker protects the circuit, and keeps tripping and resetting (clicking) as long as the short is present.
  3. Open and close the switch. Tripping even with the switch open means the short is between the fuse and the switch. Tripping only with the switch closed means the short is between the switch and the load.
  4. Disconnect connectors (or, in a real vehicle, cut or open splices) within the suspect area, one at a time. When the breaker stops clicking, the short is in the section you just disconnected.
  5. Carefully wiggle the wires in that section to find the exact spot, then repair or replace the shorted section.
Confirm it with the ohmmeter
  1. Remove the fuse (or breaker) and unplug the loads and switches in that section. Otherwise the meter reads straight through a bulb filament to ground and fools you.
  2. Connect the black lead to a clean chassis ground, and touch the red lead to the isolated wire (for example, the load side of the fuse terminal).
Fault Confirmed:0.00 Ω or a continuous beep with everything isolated. There is a direct, zero-resistance path straight to the metal frame.
Normal Reading:OL (open) or very high resistance. With the switch open and loads unplugged, there should be no path to ground.
🖥 In the simulator: the 🔧 button on a fuse installs a new fuse or a circuit breaker, and the connector tools let you disconnect individual wire ends to isolate sections.

2. Short to Power

The Goal: Find where a wire is picking up voltage from another circuit. The usual symptom is a load that will not turn off, because the short is bypassing its switch.
Mode
DC Voltage (V⎓, set to the 20V scale if not auto-ranging)
Red Lead
VΩmA jack
Black Lead
COM jack
  1. Turn the switch for the affected component OFF.
  2. Connect the black lead to a good chassis ground.
  3. Touch the red lead to the power input wire at the component, then to the switch's output terminal.
  4. If voltage is present with the switch off, disconnect sections of the circuit one at a time, working from the load back toward the switch. The section that still carries voltage while disconnected from everything else is the one touching the other circuit's power.
Fault Confirmed:12.0V to 14.4V with the switch turned completely off. The circuit is pulling power from a neighboring live wire.
Normal Reading:0.00V. There should be no voltage at the component when its switch is off.
⚠ If a different circuit turns on when you switch this one on, check for an open shared ground (feedback) before chasing a short.

3. Open Circuit

The Goal: Find where the circuit is physically broken. It's the most common fault — suspect it whenever the circuit won't turn on and the fuse is not blown.
Mode
DC Voltage (V⎓) with the circuit on (a 12-volt test light also works), then Resistance / Ohms (Ω) or Continuity (🔊) to confirm
Red Lead
VΩmA jack
Black Lead
COM jack
Find it with voltage (circuit plugged in and switched on)
  1. At the load, check the ground terminal: it should read close to 0V.
  2. Check the power terminal with the switch on: it should read close to battery voltage.
  3. Follow the wire that has the wrong voltage and test at the next access point: the other end of the wire, then each side of the switch, then the fuse. The open is between the last point with the wrong reading and the first point with the correct reading.
  4. If the power terminal and the ground terminal both read battery voltage, the open is on the ground side. With no current flowing, the load passes voltage straight through ("phantom" voltage).
Confirm it with the ohmmeter (circuit isolated)
  1. Remove power, and disconnect both ends of the suspect wire or component.
  2. Put one lead on each end of the wire and read its resistance.
Fault Confirmed:Voltage stops at the break, or OL (open) with no beep across the isolated wire. The path is physically broken.
Normal Reading:Voltage is present at every access point up to the load, and close to 0.00 Ω (typically under 0.5 Ω) end to end on a good wire.
💡 An LED test light draws very little current, so it can light even through a corroded connection and hide unwanted resistance. Use the voltmeter when the load works but works poorly.

4. Excessive Resistance

The Goal: Find hidden corrosion or loose connections that are using up voltage. The load should drop at least 98% of the battery voltage; the wires should drop almost none of it. An ohmmeter can't find this reliably because it only tests with no current flowing. The voltage drop test is the accurate way.
Mode
DC Voltage (V⎓) — Voltage Drop Test (use mV for very small drops)
Red Lead
VΩmA jack
Black Lead
COM jack
  1. Keep the circuit completely plugged in and turned ON.
  2. Measure battery voltage as your reference. Below 12V, charge the battery first, since a weak battery also makes loads weak.
  3. Measure the voltage dropped across the load (one lead on each terminal). It should be nearly the same as battery voltage.
  4. Measure the ground side drop: battery negative post to the load's ground terminal.
  5. Measure the power side drop: battery positive post to the load's power terminal.
  6. On the side with the drop, move the lead one access point at a time (each connector, each side of the switch, the fuse). The resistance is in the section where the drop disappears.
  7. Recheck across that single wire, switch, or connection. The load drop plus every wire drop should add up to the battery voltage.
Fault Confirmed:Anything above 0.5V across a wire, switch, or connection, or a load that drops noticeably less than battery voltage (e.g., a bulb dropping only 7.5V on a 12.6V system means 5.1V is being lost somewhere else).
Normal Reading:The load drops nearly all of the battery voltage, and each wire or connection drops less than 0.2V to 0.5V.

5. Verifying Your Diagnosis — Fused Jumper Wire

The Goal: Prove the repair will work before replacing parts, by testing your conclusion a second way.
Tool
Fused jumper wire (alligator clips with an inline fuse)
Works For
Open circuits and excessive resistance in wires, switches, and connections
  1. Remove or isolate the part you believe is bad first — unplug the switch, or disconnect the suspect wire at both of its connectors. If the original part is still connected, current can flow through it and the jumper at the same time, and you won't know which path made the circuit work. With the part isolated, the jumper is the only path for current.
  2. Clip the jumper into the circuit where that part was: across the switch's harness terminals, or from one end of the disconnected wire's circuit to the other.
  3. Operate the circuit.
  4. Never jumper across a load or from a power point straight to ground. With no load to limit current, it's a dead short, and the jumper's fuse will blow.
Diagnosis Verified:The circuit works (or a dim load brightens) with the jumper in place. Replacing or repairing the bypassed part will fix it.
Not Verified:No change with the jumper in place. The problem is somewhere else, so go back to your test results.
🖥 In the simulator: use the suspect part's 🔌 button to show its connectors and pull them apart. Each loose connector gets a small yellow-ringed test point on its harness side. Clip the Fused Jumper Wire (panel under the meter) onto those harness-side points to bypass the part.

6. Checking the Load Itself

The Goal: If both wires at the load have the correct voltage — full power on one side, a good ground on the other — but it still doesn't work, the load is faulty. Confirm it before replacing it.
  1. Incandescent bulb: remove it and measure resistance across the filament. OL means an open filament; anything more than a few ohms is also a failed bulb. On a dual-filament bulb, test both filaments. Don't judge a bulb by looking at it — that can fool you.
  2. LED lamp: the voltage-reducing circuit is built into the assembly. With it plugged in and turned on, check for full voltage at its connector. Full voltage but no light means the LED assembly is bad. If some LEDs light and others don't, replace the assembly.
  3. HID headlamp: confirm the ballast is receiving 12V. Never probe the high-voltage wiring between the ballast and the bulb. It can shock you and damage your meter. Swap the ballast or bulb with the other side to find which one is bad.
  4. Relay: treat the coil as its own load. Check for power on one coil terminal and ground on the other while it's commanded on. If both are correct and the contacts don't close, the relay is bad.
